analysis.one_liner: Permanently cuts the tax corporations pay on foreign profits brought home, steering half the new revenue to road and bridge repairs.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently let U.S. corporations bring foreign profits back to the United States at an effective tax rate of roughly 5%, instead of the normal 35% rate minus foreign tax credits. Half of the tax collected on those repatriated profits would go into a new Emergency Transportation Safety Fund, which the Transportation Department would spend on a prioritized list of road and bridge safety projects. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Multinational corporations holding large piles of foreign profits gain the most: they could bring that money home at a permanently reduced rate instead of paying the normal corporate rate minus foreign tax credits. States with high-priority road and bridge safety projects would gain a new funding stream, but only if corporations choose to repatriate profits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Multinationals with offshore cash; states with unsafe roads

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Emergency Transportation Safety Fund funded by half of the tax collected on repatriated foreign earnings, dedicated to road and bridge safety projects [S3].
Directs the Secretary of Transportation to rank projects by safety and traffic criteria — starting with closed interstate roads and bridges — and update the priority list publicly every quarter [S3].
Makes the reduced repatriation rate permanent and extends it to current as well as accumulated foreign earnings, not just a one-time window [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury — and by extension other taxpayers — bears the cost, since foreign profits would be taxed at a small fraction of the normal rate on a permanent basis, and the transportation fund only receives half of even that reduced revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes a roughly 5% effective rate on repatriated foreign earnings permanent, so corporations with offshore profits keep the vast majority of what they would owe under current law [S3].

Funding for the transportation fund depends entirely on corporations deciding to repatriate profits; if they do not, the fund gets nothing, and it receives only half of the tax raised when they do [S3].

The bill contains no requirement that repatriated money be invested in jobs or operations — under the structure it amends, the deduction applies to dividends received, with no use-of-funds conditions attached [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The road and bridge safety funding is a real public benefit, but it is modest and conditional compared with the tax cut: a corporation repatriating profits keeps nearly all of the tax savings, while the fund receives half of the small remaining tax. A comparable one-time repatriation holiday in 2004 (under section 965, the same provision this bill rewrites) was followed by widespread shareholder payouts rather than new investment — a well-known result that made policymakers wary of repeating it. As designed, the corporate tax reduction is the permanent, guaranteed feature; the public transportation benefit is contingent, partial, and at corporate discretion.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the 113th Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on May 9, 2013 [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No cosponsor ever signed on, and the bill took no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No corporation received the tax cut and no road fund was created. The Treasury kept current-law tax rates on foreign earnings, and multinational corporations lost out on a would-be windfall.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; corporations lost a tax windfall

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to Finance; no further action by him is recorded.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 9, 2013 and took no action on it for the rest of the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so its partisan support was a single Republican sponsor with no recorded opposition or backing.

industries.note: The bill would permanently let them bring foreign earnings home at an effective rate of about 5% instead of the normal rate minus foreign credits, keeping nearly all of the difference. The public transportation funding it offers comes only from half of the much-reduced tax they would pay.

A new dedicated fund for emergency road and bridge safety projects would mean more construction work, and the money serves the same safer roads the public wants. But the funding stream depends on voluntary corporate repatriations.

industries.industry: Foreign subsidiaries and tax-avoidance structures (controlled foreign corporations)
industries.note: Making the low repatriation rate permanent, and extending it to current earnings, would lock in the practice of holding profits offshore and waiting for repatriation windows rather than paying the standard U.S. rate.
